#### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

###### **1.1 Introduction** 

Since the release of our last 3-Year Silver Forecast in August, silver entered a brief period of rangebound trading before it took its second major hit of the year. Similar to early May, the white metal plunged by around 30% within four trading days in late September until it found support at the $30 mark.  Although the price has recovered somewhat thereafter, it has been trading at the low $30s through to end-November. 

While the silver price had shown some signs of weakness prior to the late September sell-off, the trigger for its hefty decline was the announcement of “Operation Twist” by the Fed on the 21st, which sparked fears that the government and monetary authority were running out of tools to avert a major slowdown in the world’s largest economy. 

Further downside pressure came from an escalation of E

uropean sovereign debt situation and renewed fears regarding the health of the global banking sector. Despite a new debt agreement being reached by European Union leaders on 26th October, it failed to prevent contagion fears spreading to larger economies within the region. Indeed, with political uncertainties surging in Italy and Greece in early November, the commodity and equity markets were once again under mounting strain. Finally, given silver’s notorious reputation for volatility, it is not surprising that the metal was the largest casualty across the precious metals complex, a development exacerbated by some distressed selling to raise cash for margin calls. It is of note that while we are fairly positive regarding silver in 2012, we would caution that price volatility will remain elevated and it may prove difficult to sustain investment.  In large part, this is because growing pessimism about the global economic outlook will continue to weigh on investment sentiment, whilst a stronger US dollar could also pull down industrial metal prices.  Indeed, we expect the US economy to remain sluggish next year, as an elevated unemployment, weak consumer spending and lacklasture property market will remain a drag on economic growth.  In addition, while we expect a deteriorating sovereign debt situation in Europe, as pressure now starts to affect Germany and France’s borrowing costs, European leaders may well exert intense pressure on the region’s southern countries to adopt comprehensive austerity measures. However, stabilisation of the debt problem may not start to emerge until late 2012 if not early 2013. 

This could therefore begin to reduce precious metals’ appeal as a safe haven as we move into 2013, particularly if the global economy shows clear signs of having returned to stable growth and if central banks find themselves obliged to begin a round of interest rate rises.  Nonetheless, the retreat for investment could be fairly orderly given the reluctance of some monetary authorities to tighten policy, particularly in the United States.  Furthermore, the emergence of rising inflation (perhaps more a feature for 2013), particularly in the United States will also help to limit the fall in silver prices. 

Moreover, even though economic conditions will eventually stabilise towards the end of 2013, we do not believe the initial weakness in prices then will trigger heavy net liquidation after a decade-long bull market. As such, combined with a high starting point for 2013, we still expect silver to average $38.55 that year.  Even if the boom has proved bigger and longer than we previously expected, investor interest in silver is likely to fall heavily by the end of the forecast, particularly following further improvement in the global financial and economic conditions, which will subsequently send the white metal to an average of $22.50 in 2014. 

In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two alternative scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our central forecast.  In each instance, th

A key difference between Scenario B and the Base Case is that the former assumes the persistence of sovereign debt problems for the next couple of years, rather than seeing the start of resolution next year. For example, we would not be surprised if fears regarding the breakup of the euro intensify while worries about a renewed banking crisis surge, which will finally push the ECB to start more radical bond buying. Meanwhile, facing a slowing economy, the United States may well adopt more aggressive monetary and fiscal easing, which will see the sovereign debt crisis move back to the United States and spread to Japan over the next two years. Under such circumstances, it is likely that the world economy will avoid a sharp slowdown in 2012 which should favour industrial metals. Furthermore, a more rapid increase in inflation rates seems to be inevitable, particularly in the United States where the CPI is forecast to approach 6% by 2014. This should prompt a far broader move into silver among institutional investors, which in turn will result in silver prices advancing to an average of $66.20 in 2013 before falling slightly in 2014. A complete contrast is **Scenario C** (with a 15% probability), where investment demand is forecast to peak early next year. While we could see an escalation of the European debt crisis in the near term, pressure from the bond market may well force the region’s peripheral countries to speed up on austerity plans and restore investor confidence. As more fiscal tightening measures take place next year, we expect that fears regarding the debt problem will ease considerably. Related to this is the fact that the commodity complex is likely to suffer (as a result of lower world GDP growth) under this scenario, which will then see **6** 3-Year Silver Forecast - November 2011 **CONFIDENTIAL** inflation fears eventually evaporate. These factors should reduce precious metals’ appeal to investors, most notably from mid-2012 onwards, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to l

evels that are more in line with silver’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals by 2014.  Given the heightened uncertainty and ongoing political conflicts within the Eurozone, we doubt whether a rapid and credible solution could be reached in the short term. Scenario C therefore remains the least likely outcome among the three scenarios. 

Much of the above has focused on the principal economic variables and investment.  However, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the underlying supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, if subsidiary, role in silver price determination in 2012-14. 

###### **1.2 Base Case Scenario** 

On the supply side, global **mine production** is set to post successive record highs over 2011-2014, peaking at just over 870 Moz in the final forecast year.  Growth averages 4% per annum over this period, due to a robust project pipeline, underpinned by a healthy performance from the base metal sector and further supported by healthy precious metal prices.  Since the last forecast, the series has been adjusted lower as our expectations have been moderated somewhat as greater scope for setbacks has been allowed. 

**Scrap** supply, meanwhile, is forecast to take a different path.  Following a surge to 235 Moz this year, supply flattens next year, before declining from 2013 onward. The falling profile is mostly due to steep price-led losses from jewellery and silverware, as well as ongoing declines from the photographic sector.  Losses will, however, be mitigated somewhat by underlying growth in industrial scrap.  The most notable change since the last forecast has been to scrap this year; this has been raised significantly driven by stronger jewellery and silverware scrap in response to high prices. 

With regard to **net producer hedging** , we expect some 35 Moz of supply from this source this year. Prolonged price strength in 2012 fosters another year of hedging, before lower prices in 2013 prompt a return to de-hedging. 









report has been the reduction in sales this year, due to lower than expected Russian disposals. 

On the demand side, total fabrication is set to climb by 7% from 2010 to 2014.  By far the largest component of this is **industrial** fabrication, which will reach successive record highs over the forecast.  Demand this year rises by a modest 4%, before remaining broadly flat next year as world economic growth stalls. Thereafter, gains of 5% in each of the final forecast years take the total in 2014 to almost 570 Moz, over 80 Moz higher than in 2010.  Since the last forecast, the series has been revised lower due to the downwards modification to GDP growth. 

**Jewellery** fabrication is also forecast to rise over the forecast period.  The reasons underpinning this trajectory remain unchanged since our last report, namely ongoing market penetration in the youth demograp

hic and substitution gains at the expense of gold.  The marked boost in 2013 and 2014 is a result of falling prices, coupled with improved economic growth and the resulting lift in consumer spending. **Silverware** , in contrast, will extend its long term trend of decline until 2013, before posting a modest price-led recovery in 2014, although the total remains historically low. **Photographic** demand is expected to maintain its downward trajectory, primarily as digital technology continues to erode halide technology’s share. 

Finally, demand for **coins & medals** is set to surge this year, before edging higher in 2012 to reach a new record of 145 Moz.  Although volumes will start to wane thereafter, they remain elevated. 

Overall, the forecast supply and demand figures show that the market will remain in surplus (as defined by the sum of mine production plus scrap less fabrication) until 2014.  This market surplus in the early years should be comfortably absorbed by investors whilst the economic back drop remains uncertain.  However, once this begins to improve, silver becomes vulnerable to a major correction as its supply/demand elements appear insufficiently price elastic to respond.  This actually leaves the market still dependent on a body of investors to buy up both the fundamental surplus at ever “better” prices and to absorb selling from other investors.  This uncomfortable outcome explains the persistence of implied net investment in the face of slumping prices.

Under this scenario, we assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve continue to implement loose fiscal and monetary policies. As a consequence, we expect negative real interest rates and rising inflation, with the latter reaching an annual average of 5.8% in 2014. Moving across the Atlantic, the United States’ fiscal position is actually worse than the European Union average; the US gross federal debt in 2010 was equal to 94% of the country’s GDP, while the equivalent figure for the European Union was slightly below 80%. Moreover, failure among members of the debt-reduction committee to reach agreement on how to reduce the country’s huge deficit will result in significant spending cuts, with a negative effect on growth. ###### **2.3 Base Case Scenario** Real **global** GDP growth is expected to ease to 2.8% this year, having rebounded to 5.1% in 2010. This is due to the indebted position of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world and the impact of monetary policy tightening in emerging markets. Next year, we forecast a further decline in world GDP growth to an average of 2.5%, due to a deterioration in the European sovereign debt situation. This is then followed by faster growth rates in 2013 and 2014 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and the property market, start to improve. GDP growth in the **United States** increased at an annual rate of 2.0% in the third quarter of this year. This was larg

ely due to the stronger consumer and business spending. However, economic recovery remains fragile amid a continuation of an elevated unemployment rate coupled with a lacklustre property market, both of which are likely to remain in place for an extended period. Indeed, facing a major potential in economic growth, the Federal Reserve confirmed that it would like to keep interest rate unchanged until mid2013. Furthermore, a new stimulus plan known as “Operation Twist” was announced in late September. Under this, the Fed will buy $400 billion of long-dated Treasury bonds by June 2012, while selling an equivalent amount of shorter-term securities. The plan is designed to lower long-term interest rates, while keeping shortterm rates little changed. However, as interest rates have already been cut to record lows, we doubt that this new measure of monetary stimulus will be effective in restoring consumer confidence and boosting GDP growth. Moreover, the downside risk to the US economy is growing, particularly given the failure to reach political consensus on the design of debt reduction and possible overspill from the European sovereign debt crisis. As a result, we expect US GDP growth to slow to 1.2% in the following year before economic conditions improve from 2013 onwards. Economic growth in **Europe** declined in the third quarter of 2011 on the back of the escalating debt crisis and a slowdown in economic activity in Germany and France, the two largest economies in the Eurozone. In our view, this sharp deceleration in Europe’s major economies threatens to complicate the challenge facing the region’s policy makers as they seek to deal with the escalating debt crisis. Therefore, average EU-27 growth is forecast to be around 1.4% this year. Given the excessive level of public debt in many European countries, we would expect further austerity measures to be enacted in a number of southern European countries over the next two years, which in turn will continue to reduce the region’s growth. Real GDP growth is therefore forecast to fall to 0.9% in 2012 with a possibility of outright contraction in some quarters before a gradual recovery takes place in the final two years of the forecast. Following three quarters of contraction, the **Japanese** economy grew by an annualised 6.0% in the third quarter of this year. This was largely driven by consumer spending and exports, both of which rebounded from a slump caused by the twin disasters of the earthquake and the tsunami. However, amid ongoing uncertainties in Europe and a slowdown in global growth, we expect the economy to grow at a slower rate in the final quarter of the year.
